etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
paragraphs: From Middle English rewe, rowe, rawe, from Old English rǣw, rāw, probably from Proto-Germanic *raiwō, *rīgǭ (“row, streak, line”), from Proto-Indo-European *Hreyk- (“to carve, scratch, etch”).

Cognate with Scots raw (“row”), dialectal Norwegian rå (“boundary line”), Saterland Frisian Riege (“row”), West Frisian rige (“row”), Dutch rij (“row, line”), German Low German Reeg, Riege, Rieg (“row”), German Reihe (“row”), German Riege (“sports team”).
senses: A line of objects, often regularly spaced, such as seats in a theatre, vegetable plants in a garden, etc.
A horizontal line of entries in a table, etc., going from left to right, as opposed to a column going from top to bottom.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
paragraphs: From Middle English rowen (“to row”), from Old English rōwan (“to row”), from Proto-Germanic *rōaną (“to row”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁reh₁- (“to row”). Compare West Frisian roeie, Dutch roeien, Danish ro. More at rudder. Related to Russia.
senses: (transitive or intransitive, nautical) To propel (a boat or other craft) over water using oars.
(transitive) To transport in a boat propelled with oars.
An act or instance of rowing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
paragraphs: Unclear; some suggest it is a back-formation from rouse, verb.
